title: Spin Qubits in Photon-Coupled Microwave Cavities
abstract: Electron spin qubits in microwave cavities provide a promising platform for scalable quantum computing hardware, leveraging long coherence times, charge-noise robustness and cavity mediated qubit-qubit interactions. While the strong spin-photon coupling regime is accessible via on-chip micromagnets, scaling conventional architectures by placing multiple qubits within a single shared resonator degrades transmission amplitudes, hence limiting large-scale efficiency. To overcome this limitation, we analyze a modular architecture where individual cavities containing a limited number of qubits are coupled via single-photon-exchange waveguides. Using input/output theory, we compute the transmission amplitudes for networks of two and three coupled cavities in various configurations. We map out the distinct physical regimes accessible by tuning key system parameters, offering a viable pathway for scalable cavity-based quantum spin qubit networks.
summary: This paper proposes a scalable architecture for spin qubit quantum computers by moving away from single shared resonators to modular networks of coupled microwave cavities. Using input/output theory, the authors derive transmission amplitudes for two and three connected cavities, demonstrating that this modular approach successfully mitigates signal degradation seen in conventional designs. The work provides crucial theoretical guidelines for building large-scale solid-state quantum processors.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing a scalable quantum computing platform using spin qubits coupled to microwave cavities, as conventional single shared resonators suffer from signal degradation when scaling up the number of qubits.
main_result: The authors propose and analyze a modular architecture where individual cavities are coupled via waveguides, successfully demonstrating how this approach overcomes the scalability bottleneck inherent in single-cavity designs.
method: The analysis heavily relies on input/output theory applied to open quantum systems, deriving equations of motion for cavity and qubit operators using the Lindblad master equation framework.
model_or_system: The system involves electron spin qubits realized in Double Quantum Dot (DQD) structures coupled to microwave cavities. The model is extended from single-cavity analysis to complex networks of two or three coupled cavities, utilizing specific Hamiltonian terms for coupling and qubit dynamics.
key_observables: Transmission amplitude ($A$), Rabi splitting strength ($g_s$), and the effective cavity frequency shift ($\omega_{c,	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: Tunable parameters include interdot detuning ($\epsilon$), tunnel coupling ($t_c$), and external magnetic fields ($B_z, B_x$). The analysis focuses on the resonant regime.
main_assumptions: The methodology utilizes the Rotating Wave Approximation (RWA) and treats the system as an open quantum system connected to external photon baths via input/output theory.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate transmission spectra for single-cavity systems, multi-qubit arrays in one cavity, and critically, comparative plots showing Type-A vs. Type-B coupling geometries in two and three coupled cavities.
paper_structure: The paper progresses logically from establishing the basic single-qubit/single-cavity model (using input/output theory) to analyzing the limitations of scaling within one cavity ($N$-qubits), culminating in the detailed mathematical treatment and simulation results for modular, multi-cavity networks.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles a core engineering challenge in quantum computing: connectivity. By providing analytical tools (input/output theory) to model coupled cavities, it offers a concrete pathway toward realizing large-scale solid-state quantum processors.
